steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
If somebody were going to open a store there, they would already have started publicizing it.
But there has been no such publicity.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Contrary to recent speculations, no hardware store will be opening in the shopping plaza.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion questions, listen for the conclusion early. It usually shows up in the first sentence or right after a pivot that pushes back on someone else's view.

Here the first sentence does both. "Contrary to recent speculations" tells us other people expect a hardware store, and the author is about to disagree. Then comes the author's own claim: no hardware store will be opening in the plaza.

Test it by asking, "Why should I believe that?" The next two sentences answer. Anyone opening a store there would already be publicizing it, and there has been no publicity. So nobody is opening a store there. Both sentences point back at the first one, which makes the first sentence the main conclusion and the other two its evidence.

The speculation itself is not the author's view. It is the position the author argues against.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Find the answer that restates the author's claim with the opener stripped off: a hardware store will not be opening in the shopping plaza. Expect trap answers that restate the speculation, the conditional premise, or the no-publicity premise.

notes.body: A describes the recent speculations that the author argues against. "Contrary to recent speculations" tells us the author rejects that idea, so it is the opposing point, not the conclusion.

B matches the first sentence once we drop the opener. "Contrary to recent speculations" only tells us whose view the author is rejecting; the claim itself is that no hardware store will be opening in the plaza. B says exactly that.

Run the support test: why believe B? Because anyone opening a store would already be publicizing it, and nobody is. Both premises answer the question, so B is the main point. When a conclusion arrives wrapped in a phrase that names the view being rejected, match the claim, not the wrapper.

C is the first premise: anyone opening a store there would already be publicizing it. Together with the lack of publicity, it supports the claim that no hardware store will open, so it is evidence, not the main point.

The author never says whether opening a hardware store there would be wise. The argument is a prediction about what will happen, based on the lack of publicity, not a judgment about whether it is a good idea. A Main Conclusion answer has to restate a claim the author actually made, so D is out.

E is the second premise: there has been no publicity. Paired with the claim that a store opener would already be publicizing, it is the reason no hardware store will be opening. That makes it evidence, not the main point.

steps.label: Context
steps.body:
It is a given that to be an intriguing person, one must be able to inspire the perpetual curiosity of others.

Intriguing → Inspires others' curiosity

This explains why inspiring curiosity matters. It is not offered as support for the claim that follows.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body:
Constantly broadening one's abilities and extending one's intellectual reach [perpetually expanding one's mind] will enable one to inspire that curiosity.

Expands mind → Inspires others' curiosity

steps.label: Evidence (For)
steps.body:
For such a perpetual expansion of one's mind makes it impossible to be fully comprehended, making one a constant mystery to others.

Expands mind → Not fully comprehended → Constant mystery

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion here sits in the middle sentence, and the word "For" is what gives it away. "For" means "because": the last sentence is the reason for the sentence before it. Why should we believe that expanding your mind lets you inspire curiosity? Because it makes you impossible to fully comprehend, so you stay a mystery to others.

So what is the first sentence doing? It is called "a given." Nothing argues for it, and it is not a reason for the middle sentence either. It explains why anyone would care about inspiring curiosity. That makes it background, not the conclusion.

Now the hard part: the conclusion is a conditional, so direction matters. The author says expanding your mind is enough to inspire curiosity:

Expands mind → Inspires others' curiosity

The author does not say it is the only way. An answer that flips this into a requirement, or that changes whose curiosity we are talking about, is a different claim.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that says: if you constantly broaden your abilities and extend your intellectual reach, you will be able to inspire the perpetual curiosity of others. Check the direction (broadening is the trigger, curiosity is the result) and check that the curiosity belongs to other people.

notes.body:
A restates the first sentence, the "given." Ask what it does in the argument: nothing supports it, and it is not offered as a reason for anything. It explains why inspiring curiosity matters. Background is not the main conclusion, so A is out.

Intriguing → Inspires others' curiosity

B is the middle sentence in conditional form. Broadening your abilities and extending your intellectual reach is the trigger; being able to inspire the perpetual curiosity of others is the result.

Expands mind → Inspires others' curiosity

Run the support test. Why believe B? Because constant expansion makes you impossible to fully comprehend, and so a constant mystery. The "For" sentence answers that question, so B is what the argument is built to prove. When a conclusion is a conditional, match the direction as well as the words.

C restates part of the last sentence, the one introduced by "For." That sentence is the reason for the middle claim, so C is support, not the main point. C also drops the idea of expanding one's mind, which is the trigger the conclusion is about.

Not fully comprehended → Constant mystery

D reverses the conclusion. The author says expanding your mind is enough to inspire curiosity. D says it is required: to inspire curiosity, one must constantly broaden.

Argument: Expands mind → Inspires others' curiosity
D: Inspires others' curiosity → Expands mind

Could someone inspire perpetual curiosity some other way? The argument never rules it out. D is tempting because it uses all the right words, just in the wrong direction.

This shifts whose curiosity is at stake. The argument concludes that broadening one's abilities lets one inspire the perpetual curiosity of others. This answer says one "will always have curiosity" oneself, which the argument never claims.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Many jobs require little or no creativity and, in those positions, using creativity is more likely to be disruptive than innovative. Furthermore, even if creativity were in demand, there is no evidence that it can be taught.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: There is no good reason to suppose that promoting creativity is a proper goal of an employee training program.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion questions, check the first sentence first. It is often the claim, with the reasons following it.

The manager opens with an opinion: there is no good reason to suppose promoting creativity is a proper goal of employee training. Ask, "Why should I believe that?" The rest of the paragraph answers. Reason one: many jobs need little or no creativity, and in those jobs creativity is more likely to disrupt than to innovate. Reason two, flagged by "Furthermore": even if creativity were in demand, there is no evidence it can be taught.

"Furthermore" stacks a second reason on the first. Both point back at the opening sentence, so that sentence is the main conclusion.

Notice how careful the conclusion is. The manager does not say training should never promote creativity. The claim is only that there is no good reason to think it should.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that matches the first sentence, including its caution: there is no good reason to suppose employee training programs should promote creativity. Expect traps that restate one of the two reasons, or that state them more strongly than the manager did.

notes.body: A restates the manager's first reason: in jobs that need little creativity, using it is more likely to be disruptive. That reason supports the claim that promoting creativity isn't a proper training goal, so A is a premise.

B is stronger than the manager's premise. The manager says only that there is "no evidence" creativity can be taught, not that it can't be. And that is a reason for the main point, not the main point itself.

C restates the start of the manager's first reason. Ask why we should believe the opening claim, and the fact that many jobs require little or no creativity is part of the answer. That puts C below the conclusion as support, not at the top as the main point.

D matches the first sentence. The phrase "a proper goal of an employee training program" becomes "employee training programs should promote creativity," and D keeps the manager's hedge, "no good reason to suppose." Run the support test: why believe D? Because many jobs don't need creativity, and creativity may not be teachable anyway. Both reasons support D, and D supports nothing else. That is how you confirm a main conclusion.
The manager never concedes that creativity is in demand: "even if creativity were in demand" is only a hypothetical. And even corrected, this would be a reason for the main point, not the main point.

steps.label: Opposing Point
steps.body: Many people think that if human language evolved, then something like it must be present in those species most closely related to humans, such as chimpanzees.

steps.label: Opposing Evidence
steps.body: They reason that since new traits evolve gradually, something like human language, albeit cruder, must exist in some species from which humans evolved.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: This general line of argument may be reasonable, but it simply does not follow that chimpanzees have anything like human language.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees. Chimpanzees are closely related to humans only because both evolved from a common ancestor, and the evolution of human language might easily have begun after the extinction of that common ancestor.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion questions, listen for the moment the author's own voice arrives. Here the first two sentences belong to the many people the anthropologist is answering: chimpanzees should have something like language, because traits evolve gradually and something like human language must exist in the species humans evolved from.

Then the pivot: "This general line of argument may be reasonable, but". The anthropologist grants the gradual-evolution reasoning and rejects only one step of it, the jump to chimpanzees. The claim after "but" is the author's position.

Check it with "Why should I believe that?" The answer follows the word "because": humans did not evolve from chimpanzees. Chimps are relatives through a common ancestor, and language might have started after that ancestor died out. So even if something like language must exist in species humans evolved from, chimpanzees are not one of those species, and nothing follows about them.

Notice how limited the conclusion is. The author does not say chimpanzees lack language. The claim is that this argument does not show they have it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that says the gradual-evolution reasoning does not tell us whether chimpanzees have anything like human language. The right answer may be abstract and describe the reasoning instead of quoting it. Reject any answer that says chimpanzees lack language, since the author only says it does not follow that they have it.

notes.body: A restates the anthropologist's reason, the claim after "because": humans did not evolve from chimpanzees. Its "some extinct species" reflects the common-ancestor point. Ask why the author thinks it does not follow that chimps have language, and A is the answer. That makes A evidence, not the main conclusion.

B is the conclusion in abstract form. "The assumption that something like human language must exist in some species from which humans evolved" is the reasoning the author grants. And "has no clearcut linguistic implications for chimpanzees" restates "it simply does not follow that chimpanzees have anything like human language."

B also keeps the limit: it does not say chimps lack language, only that this reasoning tells us nothing clear about them. When the right answer is abstract, translate each phrase back into the stimulus and check that the pieces line up.

C says chimpanzee communication is cruder than human language. That idea comes from the opposing reasoning ("albeit cruder"), which the anthropologist refuses to apply to chimps. The author's point is that we cannot conclude chimps have anything like human language at all, so the author never asserts C, let alone concludes it.

Intelligence never comes up. The anthropologist explains the gap with family history: humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor, and language may have started after it died out. D offers a different explanation, and it says chimpanzees lack something, which goes further than the author's claim that their having language does not follow.

E takes the last sentence and makes it stronger. The anthropologist says human language "might easily have begun" after the common ancestor died out. E says it did begin then. The author only needs the possibility to block the inference to chimpanzees, and even the softer version is a reason for the conclusion, not the conclusion.

old_steps.body: Chimpanzees are indeed closely related to humans.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees.

Human intelligence is not discussed in the argument.

A point similar to this serves as a premise in the argument. But the premise says only that human language "might easily have begun" after the extinction of that common ancestor. This answer says it did begin then, which is stronger than the premise, and a premise is not the main conclusion anyway.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body:
It's good to have national leaders voted out of office after a few years.
(*why should we believe that?*)

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body:
The reason is that reforms are generally undertaken early in a new government.
(*why should we believe that?*)

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: If leaders don't act quickly to solve a problem and it becomes an issue later, they must either deny there is a problem or deny that anything could have been done about it. Otherwise, they have to admit responsibility for the problem persisting. Waiting puts leaders in that bind, which is why reform tends to come early.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Whenever we're doing Main Conclusion, we prime our brain before reading the paragraph: "Remember, on Main Conclusion and Role, the conclusion usually appears **earlier** than its support."

For these questions, the conclusion is usually
- the first sentence
or
- a rebuttal

When we read this first sentence, we're asking ourselves, "Is this the author's conclusion? Does it sound like the pundit's opinion?"

The normative language "it is good to X" tells us that the first sentence is an opinion. If the rest of the paragraph tries to support that claim, then we'll know that the first sentence was the main conclusion.

The second sentence telegraphs that support is being provided by saying "the **reason** is that ..."

The third sentence explains why reforms come early. A leader who waits on a problem has to deny the problem, deny anything could have been done, or admit responsibility for it. Each layer supports the one above it, and the first sentence supports nothing else. That is the main conclusion.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Find an answer that says the same thing as the first sentence: it is good for national leaders to be voted out of office after a few years. Watch for answers that restate the support about reforms coming early, or that invent new claims about motivation or time in office.

notes.body: A is a claim the pundit never makes. The argument says new governments tend to reform early, not that the threat of losing office makes new leaders more motivated. A Main Conclusion answer restates a claim from the paragraph, and the conclusion here is the first sentence. A predicts a new effect instead.

B blends pieces of the evidence into a new claim. The pundit says leaders who wait must deny the problem, deny anything could be done, or admit responsibility. That is a list of options, not a claim that long-serving leaders "tend to deny responsibility." And even a fair version would be support for the first sentence, not the point it supports.

C restates the second sentence: reforms are generally undertaken early in a new government. The pundit introduces it with "The reason is that," which marks it as support for the first sentence. Ask why it is good to vote leaders out, and C is part of the answer, so it is not the conclusion.

D adds a recommendation the pundit never makes. It says leaders who act right away should get enough time to succeed, but the pundit's claim is that it is good to vote leaders out after a few years. The pundit never discusses how much time a leader needs to solve a problem, so D cannot be the claim the argument supports.

E matches the first sentence. "It is good to have national leaders voted out of office after a few years" becomes "National leaders should be removed from office every few years by the voting in of new leaders." Saying a practice is good and saying it should be done are close enough for Main Conclusion.

Run the support test: why should leaders be voted out? Because reforms come early, and leaders who wait get stuck denying problems or owning them. The rest of the paragraph supports E, and E supports nothing else.

old_steps.body:

*(why should we believe that?*)

steps.label: Context
steps.body: Many people with access to the Internet express a longing for emotional connection to a global human community, which often leads them to use the Internet to learn about other cultures.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Learning about other cultures probably will not satisfy their longing [for emotional connection].

steps.label: Evidence (for)
steps.body: The Internet is utilized primarily for acquiring information rather than developing feelings of interconnectedness.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This argument follows a pattern you will see often on Main Conclusion: setup, pivot, conclusion, reason.

The first two sentences describe what many people do: they long for a connection to a global community, so they use the Internet to learn about other cultures. Then "However" turns the paragraph. The columnist doesn't dispute that people do this; the claim is that it probably won't work. "for" then introduces the reason: the Internet is used mainly for acquiring information, not for developing feelings of interconnectedness.

Check with the support test. Why believe that learning about other cultures online won't satisfy the longing? Because the Internet is mainly an information tool. The reason fits, so the sentence between "However" and "for" is the conclusion.

Keep its boundaries in mind: it is about learning through the Internet, it is hedged with "probably," and it is about the longing for emotional connection.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Expect the correct answer to say that, for people who long for emotional connection to a global community, learning about other cultures through the Internet probably won't satisfy that longing. Keep the hedge and the Internet setting.

notes.body: A restates the first sentence: many Internet users long for emotional connection to a global community. That is the setup the columnist reacts to after "However." The columnist never argues for it; it just describes people. A claim that nothing supports and that the argument builds on is background, not the conclusion.

B restates the second sentence: the longing leads people to use the Internet to learn about other cultures. Like A, it is setup. The conclusion is the columnist's verdict on this behavior, that it probably won't satisfy the longing. B describes the behavior without the verdict.

C paraphrases the reason, the clause after "for": the Internet is used primarily for acquiring information rather than developing feelings of interconnectedness. "for" marks support. Ask why the longing won't be satisfied, and C is the answer, so it is evidence, not the main point.

D matches the sentence after "However." Its "learning about other cultures through the Internet probably will not provide emotional connection" is the columnist's "probably will not satisfy their longing." D keeps the hedge, keeps the Internet setting, and names the right people: those desiring connection to a global human community.

A useful check on Main Conclusion: when a pivot word like "However" is followed later by a support word like "for," the conclusion often sits between them.

E widens the claim. The columnist talks only about using the Internet, and the reason is tied to the Internet: it is mainly for information. E covers any "behavior that results in the acquisition of knowledge about other cultures," which would include travel or reading. E also drops "probably" and says such behavior "rarely produces" connection, a general claim the columnist never makes.

old_steps.label: Opposing Ideas
old_steps.body: Many people with access to the Internet express a longing for emotional connection to a global human community, which often leads them to use the Internet to learn about other cultures.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Learning about other cultures probably will not satisfy their longing [for emotional connection].

old_steps.label: Evidence (for)
old_steps.body: The Internet is utilized primarily for acquiring information rather than developing feelings of interconnectedness.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: This argument follows a common pattern seen in Main Conclusion questions. It starts with an Opposing Idea, followed by a pivot word. The pivot word is followed by the Conclusion, which is then followed by the Evidence. The pivot word "however" helps us spot that pattern in this argument. Also notice how the statement after "however" is a rebuttal of the statements before "however." The Conclusion of an argument is frequently a rebuttal of an Opposing Idea.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Expect the correct answer to state that learning about other cultures will not satisfy a longing for emotional connection.

old_notes.body: This answer restates the first sentence of the stimulus — that many Internet users express a longing for emotional connection to a global community. This is the opposing idea, the background context that the conclusion pushes back against. The conclusion is not that people have this longing; the conclusion is that the Internet-based approach to satisfying it will probably fail. This answer identifies a premise, not the conclusion.

This answer combines elements from the first and second sentences of the stimulus: the longing for emotional connection leads people to use the Internet to learn about other cultures. Like answer A, this is part of the opposing idea — the background that establishes what people are doing and why. The conclusion reacts to this behavior by predicting it will not work. This answer describes the setup, not the argument's response to it.

This answer closely paraphrases the evidence: the Internet is used primarily for information acquisition, with developing feelings of interconnectedness as a secondary use. This is the reason the columnist gives for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. In the argument's structure, this statement appears after the word "for" — a classic premise indicator. The conclusion is the claim this evidence supports: learning about other cultures probably will not satisfy the longing for emotional connection.

This accurately captures the argument's main conclusion. The columnist argues that people who want emotional connection to a global community will probably not get it from learning about other cultures through the Internet. This answer says essentially the same thing: for people seeking global community connection, Internet-based cultural learning probably will not provide emotional connection. It correctly targets the claim that appears between "however" (the pivot from opposing idea) and "for" (the pivot to evidence). It appropriately includes the qualifier "probably" and specifies the mechanism (learning through the Internet) without broadening to other activities.

This answer broadens the argument significantly. The columnist specifically discusses using the Internet to learn about other cultures. This answer talks more broadly about people who "engage in behavior that results in the acquisition of knowledge about other cultures" — which could include traveling, attending cultural events, reading books, and countless other activities. The argument's reasoning depends on the specific limitations of the Internet as a tool (primarily for information, not interconnectedness), so broadening beyond the Internet removes the logical foundation. Additionally, this answer does not capture the idea that the Internet's information-focused nature is the reason for the predicted failure.

steps.label: Opposing Point
steps.body: Banking industry visionaries foresee a bright day in the near future when customers will be able to transact all their financial business by means of computers or telephones from the comfort of their own homes.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: That [transacting all financial business from home by means of computers or telephones] may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: As banks eliminate their branch offices and customer-service employees, customers will have to serve as their own tellers, and pay more transaction fees for their efforts.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Main Conclusion paragraphs often open with someone else's view and then push back. This one does. The first sentence belongs to the banking industry visionaries, who see home banking as a bright day. Then "But" turns the paragraph: that may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers. That sentence is the author's own view.

Run the support test. Why believe home banking helps banks more than customers? Because banks will cut branches and staff, and customers will do the tellers' work and pay more fees for it. The last sentence answers the question, so it is evidence, and the sentence after "But" is the conclusion.

Notice the claim is a comparison (banks more than customers) and it is hedged with "may."

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: A correct answer will say that conducting all financial business from home by computer or telephone may benefit banks more than it benefits customers. Keep the comparison and the hedge.

notes.body: A restates the visionaries' forecast from the first sentence. The author brings up that view only to push back with "But." Nothing in the paragraph argues for A, and the author's own claim is about who benefits from home banking. A is the opposing view, not the conclusion.

B matches the sentence after "But." The word "that" refers back to transacting all financial business from home, and "more of a paradise for banks than for their customers" becomes "more beneficial to banks than to their customers." B keeps both the comparison and "may."

When a conclusion uses a word like "that" to point back, work out what it refers to before you match. The right answer will usually spell it out, as B does.

C restates the last sentence: as banks cut branches and staff, customers serve as their own tellers and pay more fees. Ask why home banking may favor banks over customers, and C is the answer. That makes it evidence for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

D says only that cutting branches and staff would benefit banks. The author's claim is a comparison: home banking may be better for banks than for customers. D drops the customers and the comparison, and it shifts the subject from home banking to the cuts that come with it.

E links home banking to banks eliminating branches and staff. The last sentence assumes that link, but the author never argues for it. More importantly, the conclusion is about who benefits more from home banking, and E says nothing about benefit at all.

old_steps.label: Evicence
old_steps.body: As banks eliminate their branch offices and customer-service employees, customers will have to serve as their own tellers—and pay more transaction fees for their efforts.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: A correct answer will indicate that conducting financial business from home by computer or telephone is not as beneficial for customers as it is for banks.

old_notes.body: This answer restates the opposing view presented in the first sentence of the argument — the banking industry's optimistic vision of home banking. The author introduces this view only to push back against it with "but." The conclusion is the author's own position, not the position being challenged. This answer captures the setup, not the punchline.

This answer accurately paraphrases the author's conclusion from the second sentence. The author states that home banking "may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers." This answer restates that idea: enabling home banking "may be more beneficial to banks than to their customers." The wording is different but the meaning is identical — a comparative claim that home banking disproportionately serves banks' interests. This is exactly what a correct Main Conclusion answer should do: capture the same idea in slightly different language.

This answer restates the evidence from the third sentence of the argument. The fact that customers will serve as their own tellers and pay more fees is the reason the author believes home banking benefits banks more than customers. It is the support for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. In the argument's structure, this information explains why the author holds the view expressed in the second sentence.

This answer captures only half of the conclusion. The author's point is comparative — home banking benefits banks more than customers. This answer only addresses the bank side: eliminating branches would benefit banks. It omits the customer side entirely and drops the crucial comparison. The conclusion is not just that banks will benefit; it is that banks will benefit more than customers will. Additionally, the conclusion is about the broader phenomenon of home banking, not just about eliminating branch offices specifically.

This answer cobbles together language from different parts of the argument without accurately representing any single claim the author makes. It connects home banking to the elimination of branches and employees, blending the opposing view (home banking) with the evidence (eliminating branches) into a causal claim the author never explicitly states. The conclusion is about who benefits more from home banking, not about what home banking enables banks to do. This answer sounds like it could be part of the argument, but it does not match the actual conclusion.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Many people who simply enjoy listening to popular music do not realize that it has been used to express religious and political messages.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (After all)
steps.body: Popular music has repeatedly been adopted by social movements to express their viewpoints.

steps.label: Evidence (since)
steps.body: [Popular music] has the potential to contribute to the "conversion" of nonmembers to the movement's position, as well as to raise the morale and to express the solidarity of the movement's participants.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is a three-layer argument, and the indicator words map it for us.

"After all" means the sentence that follows supports the one before it. So the first sentence is the main conclusion, and the claim that social movements have adopted popular music is support for it. Inside that sentence, "since" adds a deeper layer: movements adopt popular music because it can help convert nonmembers, raise morale and express solidarity.

Music can convert, raise morale, express solidarity
→ Social movements have adopted popular music to express their viewpoints
→ Popular music has been used for religious and political messages, which many listeners don't realize

Now look at what the support actually proves. Social movements using music to express their viewpoints shows that popular music does more than entertain. It shows nothing about what listeners realize. So the part of the conclusion the evidence backs is this: popular music has been used for something besides enjoyment. Expect the right answer to state that core in its own words.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that captures the point of the first sentence: popular music has served purposes beyond simple enjoyment, such as carrying religious and political messages. The answer may be more general than the stimulus. Watch for answers that inflate the evidence about social movements or bring in claims the author never makes.

notes.body: A takes the evidence about social movements and inflates it. The author says popular music "has the potential to contribute to" converting nonmembers and boosting morale. Contributing to a movement is not the same as accounting for its success. And even a modest version would be support for the first sentence, not the main point.

B is tempting because the first sentence mentions people who "simply enjoy" the music. But the author's claim is that these listeners miss its other uses, not that they give entertainment too much weight. Not knowing about one use is different from overvaluing another, and nothing in the paragraph argues that entertainment value is overemphasized.

C turns a modest claim, that popular music can contribute to converting nonmembers, into "the most effective way" of converting people. The author never compares popular music with any other way of winning people over. And conversion sits in the deepest layer of support, so even a fair version of C would be evidence, not the conclusion.

D states the core of the first sentence. If popular music "has been used to express religious and political messages," then it has purposes other than mere entertainment, the "simply enjoy" use the first sentence sets those messages against.

D leaves out the claim that many listeners don't realize this, but it keeps the part the evidence supports: social movements using music to spread their views shows it does more than entertain. On Main Conclusion, the right answer can be a more general restatement of the claim, as long as it says nothing the author didn't.

Emotional impact never comes up. Morale and solidarity might sound emotional, but they are listed as reasons movements adopt music, not claims about how music affects listeners in general. E's "profound emotional impact on its listeners" is a new claim the author neither states nor supports, so it cannot be the main conclusion.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Many people who simply enjoy listening to popular music do not realize that it has been used to express religious and political messages.

old_steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (After all)
old_steps.body: Popular music has repeatedly been adopted by social movements to express their viewpoints.

old_steps.label: Evidence (since)
old_steps.body: [Popular music] has the potential to contribute to the "conversion" of nonmembers to the movement's position, as well as to raise the morale and to express the solidarity of the movement's participants.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: This is a three-layer argument. The phrase "after all" tells us that what follows is support for the sentence before it — so the first sentence is the main conclusion and the "after all" clause is an intermediate conclusion. Within that clause, the word "since" introduces even deeper support — the evidence that feeds into the intermediate conclusion. The chain flows upward: music can convert/raise morale/express solidarity (premise) → social movements have adopted music (intermediate conclusion) → people don't realize music carries these messages (main conclusion). On Main Conclusion questions, identify the claim that everything else supports but that itself supports nothing further.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer that captures the main conclusion — the first sentence about people not realizing popular music has been used for religious and political messaging. Watch out for answers that restate a premise or the intermediate conclusion instead.

old_notes.body:
This answer reads more like a conclusion that could be drawn from the evidence about social movements, not the actual main conclusion about people being unaware of music's non-entertainment purposes. The argument's central claim is about the gap between perception and reality regarding popular music's purposes. The information about social movements using popular music is supporting evidence, not the overarching point. Even corrected for strength, this would describe content from the evidence rather than the main conclusion.

This answer claims that popular music "accounts for the success" of social movements — a claim far stronger than anything in the argument. The argument says popular music has been adopted by social movements because it has the potential to contribute to converting nonmembers and boosting morale. "Contributing to" and "accounting for success" are vastly different claims. The argument never suggests popular music is the reason social movements succeed; it merely observes that social movements use popular music as one tool.

The argument never discusses whether popular music's entertainment value has been "overemphasized." The argument's point is that people do not realize popular music has been used for religious and political purposes — a claim about unawareness, not about overemphasis. These are importantly different. Saying people do not know about something is not the same as saying they place too much weight on something else. The argument does not weigh entertainment value against other values or suggest that entertainment is given undue importance. It simply observes that non-entertainment uses exist and go unrecognized by many listeners.

Even corrected for strength, this would describe content from the evidence rather than the main conclusion. Conversion potential is part of the evidence explaining why social movements adopt popular music, not the argument's overarching conclusion about popular music's unrecognized non-entertainment purposes. The argument's central point is about people being unaware that popular music serves functions beyond entertainment.

This answer claims popular music is "the most effective way" of converting people to social movements — a superlative claim that goes far beyond anything in the argument. The argument says popular music has "the potential to contribute to the conversion of nonmembers," which is a modest claim about capability, not a ranking of effectiveness. The argument never compares popular music to other methods of persuasion or claims it is the best among them.

This answer correctly captures the argument's main conclusion. The argument's first sentence states that many people who enjoy popular music do not realize it has been used for religious and political messages. Paraphrased, this means popular music serves purposes beyond mere entertainment — exactly what this answer says. Everything after "after all" provides supporting evidence: social movements have adopted popular music because of its potential to convert nonmembers, raise morale, and express solidarity. These are all non-entertainment purposes, offered as reasons to believe the main claim. This answer accurately identifies the overarching point without overstating it (unlike answers that claim music "accounts for" movement success or is "the most effective" persuasion tool) and correctly targets the conclusion rather than the evidence or an out-of-scope claim.

The argument never discusses popular music's emotional impact on listeners. While one might reasonably believe that popular music has a profound emotional impact, the argument is specifically about popular music being used for religious and political messages by social movements. The evidence discusses converting nonmembers, raising morale, and expressing solidarity — these are functional purposes related to social advocacy, not a general claim about emotional depth. "Profound emotional impact" is a separate characteristic of music that the argument neither asserts nor addresses. The main conclusion is about unrecognized non-entertainment purposes, not about emotional effects.
